title: Magha Puja
hook: in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, the February or March full moon: 1,250 disciples gather unannounced

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asalha Puja: the Deer Park, the five ascetics, the four truths, the wheel set rolling. Your line was the wheel still turns. Did you see the truths at work in your day? Day one hundred fifty, the last of the holy days.

No group chat. No invitation. No reminder the day before. And still, everyone who mattered walks through the door. In ordinary life it hardly ever works that way. Tradition tells of a full moon when it did, on a remarkable scale. Twelve hundred and fifty monks walked to the same grove on the same night, the story goes, and not one of them had been called. Today: the full moon that remembers them.
screen: `NO INVITATION, NO REMINDER.` → `EVERYONE WALKS IN ANYWAY.` → `1,250, UNCALLED.`

segments.voice: Magha Puja. Magha is the month whose full moon falls in February or March. It's kept especially in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. The story, as the commentaries tell it, happened at the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha, in the first year of the Buddha's teaching. Four things came together, which is why the day is sometimes called the fourfold assembly. It was the full moon of Magha. Twelve hundred and fifty monks arrived without being summoned. All of them were arahants, fully awakened. And all had been ordained by the Buddha himself. To that gathering, the tradition says, the Buddha gave a short summary of the whole teaching, called the Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation. Its heart is a verse in the Dhammapada. In Max Muller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind", that, the verse says, is the teaching of the awakened ones. Three parts. One common reading: the first is the precepts, the second is giving and kindness, the third is meditation. Some teachers call it the whole teaching small enough to fit on a sticky note. On Magha Puja night in Thailand, people gather at temples at dusk and walk around the main hall three times, holding a candle, incense and flowers, one circle each for the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha. Some Western communities keep a Sangha Day of their own in the same spirit. So look back over this week of holy days. Vesak: born, awake, gone. Hanamatsuri: a clean beginning. Lanterns: light for the many. Culture or religion: both. The wheel still turns. And tonight, the sangha, the people who came without being called.
screen: `MAGHA: THE FEB-MARCH MOON.` · `FOUR THINGS AT THE BAMBOO GROVE.` · `NO SIN, DO GOOD, PURIFY THE MIND.` · `THREE CIRCLES WITH A CANDLE.` · then, large: `THEY CAME WITHOUT BEING CALLED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Picture the Bamboo Grove at moonrise, and monks walking in from every direction, quietly, taking their seats. Now bring to mind the people who practice alongside you, near or far: a friend, a teacher, a stranger at a temple, anyone doing this same thing today. Let them take their seats in the grove, too. Rest in that company. Then choose one person you might practice with today, even for five minutes. The bell holds the time.
Magha Puja. The full moon of Magha, remembering twelve hundred and fifty awakened monks who gathered without being called, and the verse at the heart of the teaching.
Your line: they came without being called. Today, practice with someone: sit together, walk together, or send a friend a message to sit at the same time. Day one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: On Magha Puja, especially in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Buddhists gather at temples at dusk and walk three times around the main hall carrying a candle, incense and flowers, and many keep the eight precepts and listen to teaching.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the month of Magha, whose full moon falls in February or March.

trapdoor: what you thought: another full-moon holiday.
what it means: the day of the sangha, and of the teaching summed up in three lines.
what a scholar hears: the four factors (caturangasannipata) come from the commentaries; Dhammapada 183–185 preserve the Ovada Patimokkha verses, also found in DN 14.

Commentarial tradition of the fourfold assembly (caturangasannipata) at Veluvana

notes: Please check Max Muller's wording of Dhammapada 183 as quoted (the verse continues 'that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened').
The four factors and the setting (Veluvana, first year of teaching) come from the commentaries, and the script says 'as the commentaries tell it'; confirm.
The candlelit circumambulation (wian thian in Thai) is general; confirm.

Reviewer change: the script no longer says Western communities 'call it Sangha Day'. Some Western groups (e.g. Triratna) keep a Sangha Day, but often on a different full moon (November), so it is now described as 'a Sangha Day of their own in the same spirit'; confirm.
Reviewer change: the hook's 'on a scale nobody has matched since' was softened to 'on a remarkable scale', since that superlative cannot be verified.
The 1,250 are traditionally all arahants ordained by the Buddha; this is presented as the tradition's account, not as historical fact.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know the feeling' (banned opener, and it told the listener what they feel); dropped the unsourced 'from all over the region'; the precepts/kindness/meditation reading of Dhp 183 is now 'one common reading', and 'many Buddhists would write that verse' became 'some teachers call it'; fork no longer asks what 'many Buddhists choose'; replaced the stock 'you're not sitting alone' in the practice.
